notes.text: Up, make us gods which shall go before us. They were weary of waiting for the promised land. They thought themselves detained too long at Mount Sinai. They had a God that stayed with them, but they must have a God to go before them to the land flowing with milk and honey. They were weary of waiting for the return of Moses: As for this Moses, the man that brought us up out of Egypt, we know not what is become of him — Observe how slightly they speak of his person, this Moses: And how suspiciously of his delay, we know not what is become of him. And they were weary of waiting for a divine institution of religious worship among them, so they would have a worship of their own invention, probably such as they had seen among the Egyptians. They say, make us gods which shall go before us. Gods! How many would they have? Is not one sufficient? And what good would gods of their own making do them? They must have such Gods to go before them as could not go themselves farther than they were carried!

And Aaron said break off the golden ear-rings — We do not find that he said one word to discountenance their proposal. Some suppose, that when Aaron bid them break off their ear-rings, he did it with design to crush the proposal, believing that, though their covetousness would have let them do it, yet their pride would not have suffered them to part with them.

And all the people brake off their ear-rings — Which Aaron melted down, and, having a mold prepared, poured the melted gold into it, and then produced it in the shape of an ox or calf, giving it some finishing strokes with a graving tool.

And Aaron built an altar before it, and proclaimed a feast — A feast of dedication; yet he calls it a feast to Jehovah; for, as brutish as they were, they did not design to terminate their adoration in the image; but they made it for a representation of the true God, whom they intended to worship in and through this image. And yet this did not excuse them from gross idolatry, no more than it will excuse the Papists, whose plea it is, that they do not worship the image, but God by the image; so making themselves just such idolaters as the worshippers of the golden calf, whose feast was a feast to Jehovah, and proclaimed to be so, that the most ignorant and unthinking might not mistake it.

And they rose up early on the morrow, and offered sacrifice to this new made deity. And the people sat down to eat and drink of the remainder of what was sacrificed, and then rose up to play — To play the fool, to play the wanton. It was strange that any of the people, especially so great a number of them, should do such a thing. Had they not, but the other day, in this very place, heard the voice of the Lord God speaking to them out of the midst of the fire, Thou shalt not make to thyself any graven image? - Yet They made a calf in Horeb, the very place where the law was given It was especially strange that Aaron should be so deeply concerned, should make the calf and proclaim the feast! Is this Aaron the saint of the Lord! Is this he that had not only seen, but had been employed in summoning the plagues of Egypt, and the judgments executed upon the gods of the Egyptians? What! And yet himself copying out the abandoned idolatries of Egypt? How true is it, that the law made them priests which had infirmity, and needed first to offer for their own sins?

They have turned aside quickly — Quickly after the law was given them, and they had promised to obey it; quickly after God had done such great things for them, and declared his kind intentions to do greater.
It is a stiff-necked people — Unapt to come under the yoke of the divine law, averse to all good, and prone to evil, obstinate to the methods of cure.

Let me alone — What did Moses, or what could he do, to hinder God from consuming them? When God resolves to abandon a people, and the decree is gone forth, no intercession can prevent it. But God would thus express the greatness of his displeasure, after the manner of men, who would have none to interceed for those they resolve to be severe with. Thus also he would put an honour upon prayer, intimating, that nothing but the intercession of Moses could save them from ruin, that he might be a type of Christ, by whose mediation alone God would reconcile the world unto himself.

And Moses besought the Lord his God — If God would not be called the God of Israel, yet he hoped he might address him as his own God. Now Moses is standing in the gap to turn away the wrath of God. Psalm cvi, 23. He took the hint which God gave him when he said, Let me alone, which, though it seemed to forbid his interceding, did really encourage it, by shewing what power the prayer of faith hath with God.

Turn from thy fierce wrath — Not as if he thought God were not justly angry, but he begs that he would not be so greatly angry as to consume them. Let mercy rejoice against judgment; repent of this evil - Change the sentence of destruction into that of correction, against thy people which thou broughtest up out of Egypt - For whom thou hast done so great things? Wherefore should the Egyptians say, For mischief did he bring them out - Israel is dear to Moses, as his kindred, as his charge; but it is the glory of God that he is most concerned for. If Israel could perish without any reproach to God's name, Moses could persuade himself to sit down contented; but he cannot bear to hear God reflected on; and therefore this he insists upon, Lord, What will the Egyptians say? They will say, God was either weak, and could not, or fickle, and would not compleat the salvation he begun.
Remember Abraham — Lord, if Israel be cut off, what will become of the promise?

And the Lord repented of the evil he thought to do — Though he designed to punish them, yet he would not ruin them. See here, the power of prayer, God suffers himself to be prevailed with by humble believing importunity. And see the compassion of God towards poor sinners, and how ready he is to forgive.

glossa.text: *Make us,* etc. Gods in the plural, although one calf only was made, after the likeness, namely, of the ox Apis, whom they worshipped in Egypt; but he who cultivates idolatry subjects himself to all vices, and serves as many gods and demons as vices.

*And Aaron said to,* etc. *(AUG., quaest. 141 in Exod.)* Aaron is understood to command hard things, that in this way he might call them back from that purpose. Yet that very hard thing was done, that there might be gold for the making of the idol: which I thought was to be noted on account of those who are grieved if they are bidden to have any such thing divinely done for eternal life, or to bear it with an even mind.

*And the people sat down to eat,* etc. Eating and drinking drove them to play, and play to idolatry: because if the fault of vanity is not warily restrained, the unwary mind is devoured by iniquity. Whence: *He that despises little things, falls little by little.* For if we neglect to care for small things, being insensibly seduced, we boldly perpetrate even greater ones.

*These are thy gods. ((AUG., quaest. 142.))* The Lord, showing to Moses what the people had done concerning the calf and concerning the idol which they had made out of their own gold, says that they had said: These are thy gods, O Israel, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt. Which it is not read that they said; but God showed that this was their mind, for they bore in their heart the sense of these words, which could not lie hid from God.

*Let me alone,* etc. ((GREG., lib. IX Moral., cap. 11.)) What is it to say to a servant, etc., *as far as* he could not temper the anger of God for himself.

((ID., lib. XX Moral., cap. 6.)) It can build up the reader according to the history, etc., *as far as* nor mercy of discipline.

*Remember Abraham, Isaac,* etc. He brings in the fathers, who are loved, on behalf of the sons, who offend, and do not deserve to be heard; because the good things of the holy fathers often come to the aid of the sons.

*And the Lord was appeased that he would not do the evil.* ((AUG.)) By malice he wished punishment to be understood here, as is that: The malice of their going out was esteemed. According to this both good and evil are said to be from God, not according to the malice by which men are evil. For God is not evil: but he brings evils upon the evil, because he is just.

notes.text: Me — He speaks here in the name, and on the behalf of the whole nation. With-With those favours which thou dost usually and peculiarly give to thy people.

See — Enjoy. Chosen - Of thy chosen people; such as are Israelites indeed. Gladness - Such joy as thou hast formerly afforded unto thy beloved nation. Glory - That we may have occasion to glory in God's goodness towards us. Inheritance - In the congregation of thy people.
Glory — As our fathers did.

A calf — When they were but just brought out of Egypt by such wonders, and had seen the plagues of God upon the Egyptian idolaters, and when the law of God was but newly delivered to them in such a tremendous manner.
Their glory — God, who was indeed their glory. Into - Into the golden image of an ox or calf, which is so far from feeding his people, as the true God did the Israelites, that he must be fed by them.

Breach — God had made a wall about them; but they had made a breach in it by their sins, at which the Lord, who was now justly become their enemy, might enter to destroy them; which he had certainly done, if Moses by his prevailing intercession had not hindered him.

glossa.text:
*Alleluia. Alleluia.* Some say that one *alleluia* belongs to the end of the preceding psalm, and the other to the following. For Jerome hands down that this rule is to be held. To whose assertion Cassiodorus also agrees. But the greater number assign it, wherever alleluia stands, to the psalm that follows: and sometimes once, sometimes twice; as the Lord in the Gospel now said *amen,* now *amen amen,* for the greater certainty of the matter. With these Augustine agrees, especially since no codices of the Greeks have alleluia at the end of a psalm.

*Give glory to the Lord.* ((AUG.)) This psalm is joined to the preceding, etc., *as far as* he admonishes therefore to a twofold confession, of praise and of sins.

((CASS.)) The Hebrew, having left the perfidy of his fathers and being turned to the mercy of God, persuades others to be turned to the same mercy, praying that they may be joined to the well-pleasing people, which was to be gathered at the coming of Christ.
*Who shall declare.* ((CASS.)) He that asks for mercy is filled with the consideration of the divine works, and marvelling says: *Who shall declare?*
*Blessed are they that keep.* ((AUG.)) Or because there follows, etc., *as far as* judgment and justice, because *Blessed are they that,* etc.

*To see,* etc. ((AUG.)), that we may see thee in that goodness which thou bestowest upon the elect, that is, by thy grace let us see, lest we remain blind. *That thou mayest be praised:* it is strange that in very many codices, etc., *as far as* because he is not praised save on account of thee.

*We have sinned.* The second part, where he enumerates the sins of the fathers which they committed in Egypt, and yet says that they were delivered by God.

*Iniquity.* ((CASS.)) A third time he says the same, that the confession may appear pure; a man is loosed the more quickly, the more keenly he condemns himself.

*And they made.* ((CASS.)) Not enduring the absence of Moses, while he himself tarried on the top of mount Sinai to receive the law, they made a calf. *Horeb.* It is interpreted *Calvary,* where the crucifixion took place, etc., *as far as* this the impatience of the fickle did, as all evils are born of it.
*In the likeness.* ((AUG.)) He does not say into a likeness, but in a likeness. And it is such a manner of speech as above, *and they believed in his words.*

*They forgot.* ((CASS.)) Great forgetfulness indeed in the memory, if not the deliverance.

*Terrible things.* Because they afflicted their adversaries, and showed to these men whom they ought to fear.

*Had stood in the breach.* ((AUG.)) Saying: *If thou forgive them not, blot me out of thy book.* How much avails the intercession of the saints? Moses, secure concerning the justice of God, by which he could not blot him out, obtained mercy for those who would justly have perished.

*That he might turn away his wrath.* Concerning the water of contradiction and the immolation of the sons, whereat God was the more vehemently angered, and yet afterwards had mercy. *And for nothing.* The fourth part, where he likewise enumerates yet other sins, and says that God was appeased through Phinees.

*They believed not his word.* ((AUG.)) They despised that which was signified by her, etc., *as far as* they did not await his counsel.

*In his tents.* ((CASS.)) They murmured, because this befalls not them that labour but the idle, whence the greater odium of the crime grows.

notes.text: So stand — As ye have done hitherto.
I beseech — He repeats this twice, as if speaking to each face to face, and that with the utmost tenderness.

And I entreat thee also, true yokefellow — St. Paul had many fellowlabourers, but not many yokefellows. In this number was Barnabas first, and then Silas, whom he probably addresses here; for Silas had been his yokefellow at the very place, Acts xvi, 19. Help those women who laboured together with me - Literally, who wrestled. The Greek word doth not imply preaching, or anything of that kind; but danger and toil endured for the sake of the gospel, which was also endured at the same time, probably at Philippi, by Clement and my other fellowlabourers - This is a different word from the former, and does properly imply fellowpreachers. Whose names, although not set down here, are in the book of life - As are those of all believers. An allusion to the wrestlers in the Olympic games, whose names were all enrolled in a book. Reader, is thy name there? Then walk circumspectly, lest the Lord blot thee out of his book!

Let your gentleness — Yieldingness, sweetness of temper, the result of joy in the Lord. Be known - By your whole behaviour. To all men - Good and bad, gentle and froward. Those of the roughest tempers are good natured to some, from natural sympathy and various motives; a Christian, to all. The Lord - The judge, the rewarder, the avenger. Is at hand - Standeth at the door.

Be anxiously careful for nothing — If men are not gentle towards you, yet neither on this, nor any other account, be careful, but pray. Carefulness and prayer cannot stand together. In every thing - Great and small. Let your requests be made known - They who by a preposterous shame or distrustful modesty, cover, stifle, or keep in their desires, as if they were either too small or too great, must be racked with care; from which they are entirely delivered, who pour them out with a free and filial confidence. To God - It is not always proper to disclose them to men. By supplication - Which is the enlarging upon and pressing our petition. With thanksgiving - The surest mark of a soul free from care, and of prayer joined with true resignation. This is always followed by peace. Peace and thanksgiving are both coupled together, Colossians iii, 15.

And the peace of God — That calm, heavenly repose, that tranquility of spirit, which God only can give. Which surpasseth all understanding - Which none can comprehend, save he that receiveth it. Shall keep - Shall guard, as a garrison does a city. Your hearts - Your affections. Your minds - Your understandings, and all the various workings of them; through the Spirit and power of Christ Jesus, in the knowledge and love of God. Without a guard set on these likewise, the purity and vigour of our affections cannot long be preserved.

Finally — To sum up all. Whatsoever things are true - Here are eight particulars placed in two fourfold rows; the former containing their duty; the latter, the commendation of it. The first word in the former row answers the first in the latter; the second word, the second and so on. True - In speech. Honest - In action. Just - With regard to others. Pure - With regard to yourselves. Lovely - And what more lovely than truth? Of good report - As is honesty, even where it is not practiced. If there be any virtue - And all virtues are contained in justice. If there be any praise - In those things which relate rather to ourselves than to our neighbour. Think on these things - That ye may both practice them yourselves, and recommend them to others.

The things which ye have learned — As catechumens. And received - By continual instructions. And heard and seen - In my life and conversation. These do, and the God of peace shall be with you - Not only the peace of God, but God himself, the fountain of peace.

glossa.text: *Joy, and consolation.* That is, through whom I am gladdened in the present and shall be crowned in the future. For when the disciples are victors in the contest, the master will be worthy of the crown.
*I beseech Evodia,* etc. I admonish all, but especially Evodia and Syntyche: because these religious women were wont to receive preachers.

*Names.* They who are distinguished by merits shall have diverse mansions in the eternal house. Whence: *In my Father's house there are many mansions ((Joan. XIV))*. *The book of life.* The predestination in which all who are to be saved have been predestined. As if: Do not, O Philippians, take it hard that I have not named you all one by one in my epistle, for although you are not written in it, yet in the book of life you are contained.

*Rejoice,* etc. Being gladdened over their faith and their works, the Apostle, that they may be the more eager, desires that they, advancing in this zeal, should rejoice in the Lord, and he repeats it, that he may show that he truly rejoices in them.

*Moderation.* That is, right measure, so that all joy may be in the Lord, and that others may learn this through you. Or, *let moderation be known to all,* faithful and unbelieving, that they may imitate it, lest they be able to reprehend. *The Lord is nigh,* that is, ready to give whatsoever is needful in spiritual or in temporal things. Be solicitous and fearful about nothing. But your petitions concerning those things which you wish to obtain.

*But in every prayer.* Prayer and supplication are made in common for oneself or for others, concerning whatsoever things, but petition is made concerning things necessary by name. *Let them be made known.* This making known comes about by assiduity, and by watchfulness of prayer. Then at last peace keeps the hearts in Christ. He says this for this reason, because he who has peace with God does not fear an adverse mind. *With God.* Or to the angels, who offer them to God. Whence: When you were praying, I offered your prayer before God. Or, let them be made known for us with God through endurance, not with men through boasting.

*And the peace of God,* that is, God, who is the highest peace, which cannot even be thought, and therefore outside him there is need of nothing. *It surpasseth all understanding.* Ours, not that of those who always behold the face of the Father. Or, the peace whereby God himself is at peace *surmounts all understanding:* except his own, because neither can we know it thus, nor can any angels.

*For the rest, brethren,* etc. Thus far he has admonished against persecutors and against false preachers. But for the rest, in the conclusion, he sets forth the things which belong to perfection. *Whatsoever things are just.* This toward one's neighbour. *Holy,* in one's own life; and, that a lesser thing be named, *whatsoever things are lovely,* that is, worthy to be loved, as a modest gait, humble speech and the like.

*Of good report. ((AUG.))* For ourselves our own life, for others a good report is necessary. Accordingly whosoever guards his life from the crimes of shameful deeds does well to himself; but whosoever [guards] his good report is merciful toward others also.

notes.text: Jesus answering, spake — That is, spake with reference to what had just past.
A king, who made a marriage feast for his son — So did God, when he brought his first - begotten into the world.
Them that were invited — Namely, the Jews.
Fatlings — Fatted beasts and fowls.
One to his farm, another to his merchandise — One must mind what he has; another, gain what he wants. How many perish by misusing lawful things!
The king sending forth his troops — The Roman armies employed of God for that purpose. Destroyed those murderers - Primarily the Jews.
Go into the highways — The word properly signifies, the by- ways, or turnings of the road.
They gathered all — By preaching everwhere.
The guest — The members of the visible Church.
A wedding garment — The righteousness of Christ, first imputed, then implanted. It may easily be observed, this has no relation to the Lord's Supper, but to God's proceeding at the last day.
Many are called; few chosen — Many hear; few believe. Yea, many are members of the visible, but few of the invisible Church. Matt. xx, 16.

glossa.text: *It was made like.* Again he convicts them by parables: he is not silent because they are exasperated, but by another parable he tells them that a worse anger of God is to come. *A marriage feast.* The bridal chamber of the marriage is the virgin's womb. Of those invited to the marriage Matthew alone tells. Luke tells another likeness in part, of a supper, that is, of the eternal banquet, from which no one who has entered is driven out, as he is from the present Church.

*The oxen.* Because first the prophets, and afterwards the apostles, suffered from unbelievers: who are now to you for an example of what you must believe. Come, by faith, by agreeing with the rest. The oxen are the fathers of the Old Testament, to whom leave was granted to strike their enemies as with a horn. The fatlings, from feeding, that is, the heralds of the New Testament, fat with inward charity, seeking things on high on the wing of contemplation. Slain, either from what they had been, or already set in rest through the death of the flesh.
*Another to his farm.* To go to a farm is to lie immoderately upon earthly labour. But to trade is to gape after earthly gains.

*And the king.* Above, he was a man while he was inviting and doing works of clemency, now in taking vengeance he is king only . *And having sent,* etc. Having sent his armies, that is, the angels by whom he will exercise judgment, he destroys the persecutors: and the city, that is, the flesh in which they dwelt, he will burn with the soul in hell.

*The marriage indeed is ready.* The whole sacrament of the incarnation is accomplished, the nativity and the passion.

*To the outgoings,* etc. Actions are the ways: the outgoings are the failing of actions: because for the most part those are easily converted whom no prosperity attends in earthly doings.

*That he might see the guests.* That is, that he may make the merits of those to be judged be seen, and may discern them. *Not clothed with a wedding garment.* Now, the Pharisees having been refuted, he adds that not all who are in the Church are worthy of the kingdom, lest his own grow slothful.
*Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment?* A friend, because invited to the marriage. *How,* he convicts him of shamelessness.

*His hands and feet being bound.* They are bound by punishment who here would not be bound from evil, that is, restrained. The hands which were not stretched out to almsgiving. The feet slow to good. There each several member shall be subjected to punishments, which here served each several vice. *Outer,* etc. Because here they have the inward darkness of the heart.

*But many are called, but few chosen.* One being cast out, in whom the whole body of the wicked is set forth, a general sentence is brought in. *But many are called.* As though he should say: Even if I have spoken of one, it is to be understood of many.

echoes.text: The crowns shall be to Helem, and to Tobijah, and to Jedaiah, and to Hen the son of Zephaniah, for a memorial in Yahweh’s temple.
echoes.note: Paul's calling the Philippians his 'crown' (stephanos) echoes the prophetic image of a crown laid up as a memorial and reward in the temple, and more broadly the OT crown-of-glory motif (Isaiah 28:5; 62:3). Volume is faint and the metaphor is conventional, but coherence with the eschatological reward imagery available in the prophets supports a low-grade echo.

echoes.text: You shall also be a crown of beauty in the hand of Yahweh, and a royal diadem in the hand of your God.
echoes.note: 'You shall be a crown of beauty in the hand of the LORD' supplies the figural background for Paul's 'my joy and crown,' where a redeemed community is the eschatological adornment of its caretaker. Recurrence of the crown-of-glory image across Isaiah (28:5; 62:3) makes it available, though the volume here is low and the trope generic.

echoes.text: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers;
echoes.note: The exhortation to 'stand firm in the Lord' draws on the OT contrast between the stable righteous, planted and unmoved, and the chaff-like wicked. Coherence with the steadfastness motif (Psalm 1:3; 112:6) is real, but the volume is faint and 'stand firm' is too diffuse to anchor a single source, so this is a contested echo.

echoes.text: Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin—and if not, please blot me out of your book which you have written.”
echoes.note: Paul's claim that his fellow workers' 'names are in the book of life' alludes directly to Moses' plea to be blotted out of 'the book you have written,' the founding OT text of the heavenly register. Volume is high (the explicit book-of-life image), availability is secure in the Torah, and coherence with Paul's confidence in the Philippians' salvation is strong.

echoes.text: Let them be blotted out of the book of life, and not be written with the righteous.
echoes.note: 'Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not enrolled among the righteous' provides the precise phrase 'book of life/living' that Paul reverses into a positive assurance. High volume on the shared lexeme, strong recurrence of the register motif across the Psalter and prophets, and thematic coherence with the contrast of the saved versus the lost.

echoes.text: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book.
echoes.note: Daniel's eschatological promise that 'everyone whose name is found written in the book' shall be delivered supplies the apocalyptic deliverance sense Paul gives the image. Availability in Second-Temple apocalyptic and coherence with the resurrection hope of Philippians 3 make this a strong contributor to Paul's 'book of life.'

echoes.text: Then those who feared Yahweh spoke one with another; and Yahweh listened, and heard, and a book of memory was written before him, for those who feared Yahweh, and who honored his name.
echoes.note: 'A book of remembrance was written before him of those who feared the LORD' offers the motif of a heavenly ledger recording the faithful by name, coherent with Paul's naming of co-laborers whose names stand recorded. Volume is moderate (remembrance-book rather than 'book of life'), but recurrence within the register tradition supports the link.

echoes.text: You number my wanderings. You put my tears into your bottle. Aren’t they in your book?
echoes.note: 'Are they not in your book?' adds another instance of the divine record motif, reinforcing the availability and recurrence of the heavenly-book tradition Paul invokes. Low volume and no shared 'life' lexeme make it a faint contributing echo rather than a primary source.

echoes.text: Yahweh is near to all those who call on him, to all who call on him in truth.
echoes.note: 'The Lord is at hand' (ho kyrios engys) most closely matches 'The LORD is near to all who call on him' (engys kyrios), grounding Paul's nearness claim and its link to prayer in v.6. High lexical volume on engys, coherence with the prayer/petition context, and availability in the LXX Psalter make this the strongest source for the phrase.

echoes.text: Be glad in Yahweh, and rejoice, you righteous! Shout for joy, all you who are upright in heart!
echoes.note: 'Rejoice in the LORD always' echoes the recurrent Psalter imperative 'Be glad in the LORD, and rejoice, you righteous' (32:11; cf. 33:1; 97:12). Recurrence is strong across the Psalter and coherence with Paul's joy theme is high; volume is moderate because Paul universalizes 'always' beyond any single psalm.

echoes.text: Be glad in Yahweh, you righteous people! Give thanks to his holy Name.
echoes.note: 'Rejoice in the LORD, O you righteous' supplies the same divine-object joy imperative that Paul doubles for emphasis. The Psalter's habitual call to rejoice in the LORD is available and coherent, though the volume of any single verse is moderate given the formula's diffusion.

echoes.text: Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.
echoes.note: 'The LORD is near to the brokenhearted' reinforces the 'Lord is near' motif with the same engys idiom, and Psalm 34 broadly underwrites Paul's confidence in deliverance. Recurrence of the nearness formula with Psalm 145 strengthens coherence, though volume per verse is moderate.

echoes.text: Be silent at the presence of the Lord Yahweh, for the day of Yahweh is at hand. For Yahweh has prepared a sacrifice. He has consecrated his guests.
echoes.note: 'The day of the LORD is at hand/near' supplies the eschatological-imminence sense of 'The Lord is at hand,' if Paul means the Lord's coming rather than his presence. Availability in the prophetic day-of-the-Lord tradition and coherence with Philippians' Parousia hope (3:20) support this, though it competes with the Psalter nearness reading.

echoes.text: You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.
echoes.note: 'You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you' parallels Paul's 'peace of God which surpasses all understanding will guard your hearts,' linking divine peace, the mind, and protective keeping. Coherence is strong on the guarding-peace-of-the-mind motif; volume is moderate because Paul does not quote the phrasing verbatim.

echoes.text: Cast your burden on Yahweh, and he will sustain you. He will never allow the righteous to be moved.
echoes.note: 'Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you' parallels Paul's remedy for anxiety: hand your requests to God in prayer rather than carry them. Coherence with the anti-anxiety-through-petition logic is strong; volume is moderate since Paul shares the idea, not the wording.

echoes.text: In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you, Yahweh alone, make me live in safety.
echoes.note: 'In peace I will both lie down and sleep, for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety' offers the OT pairing of divine peace with security from anxiety that underlies 'do not be anxious... and the peace of God will guard you.' Volume is low and the link thematic, so this is a contributing echo.

echoes.text: Anxiety in a man’s heart weighs it down, but a kind word makes it glad.
echoes.note: 'Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad' supplies a wisdom backdrop for Paul's 'in nothing be anxious.' Volume and verbal overlap are slight, but the heart-anxiety theme is available in the sapiential tradition, making this a faint echo.

echoes.text: And if a man loves righteousness, The fruits of wisdom’s labor are virtues, For she teaches soberness and understanding, righteousness and courage; And there is nothing in life for men more profitable than these.
echoes.note: Wisdom's praise of the cardinal virtues ('she teaches self-control and prudence, justice and courage') models the Hellenistic-Jewish virtue list Paul adapts, especially the terms for 'just' and the framing of virtue (arete) itself, which Paul uses uniquely here. Coherence with the Wisdom tradition's moral catalogues makes this a plausible deuterocanonical source.

echoes.text: He who loves purity of heart and speaks gracefully is the king’s friend.
echoes.note: Paul's virtue catalogue (true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, of good report) draws on the sapiential ideal of the pure heart and gracious speech that wins favor. Recurrence of these virtue terms in Proverbs and the wider Hellenistic-Jewish moral tradition supplies availability, but the volume of any one verse is low.

echoes.text: So you will find favor, and good understanding in the sight of God and man.
echoes.note: 'So you will find favor and good repute (LXX: good things) in the sight of God and man' parallels Paul's 'whatever is of good report' and the appeal to public commendation. Volume is low and the link conceptual, but the good-repute motif is available in the sapiential tradition.

echoes.text: You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.
echoes.note: 'The God of peace will be with you' continues the divine-peace motif of v.7 and resonates with Isaiah's promise that God keeps in peace those whose minds are fixed on him. Volume is faint here and the title 'God of peace' is Paul's own, so this is a low-grade continuation echo of the peace tradition.

echoes.text: Then Gideon built an altar there to Yahweh, and called it “Yahweh is Peace.” To this day it is still in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
echoes.note: Gideon's altar 'The LORD is peace' (YHWH-shalom) offers an OT antecedent for naming God by his peace, loosely behind Paul's 'the God of peace.' The volume is very low and the connection figural, but it documents the availability of associating God's name with shalom.

echoes.text: In this mountain, Yahweh of Armies will make all peoples a feast of fat things, a feast of choice wines, of fat things full of marrow, of well refined choice wines.
echoes.note: The eschatological banquet — the LORD makes 'a feast of fat things' (fatlings/oxen killed, 22:4) for all peoples on his mountain. The king's marriage feast for his son draws on this prophetic image of the messianic/end-time banquet; the killing of fatlings matches Isaiah's 'fat things full of marrow.'

echoes.text: Be silent at the presence of the Lord Yahweh, for the day of Yahweh is at hand. For Yahweh has prepared a sacrifice. He has consecrated his guests. It will happen in the day of Yahweh’s sacrifice, that I will punish the princes, the king’s sons, and all those who are clothed with foreign clothing.
echoes.note: The LORD 'has prepared a sacrifice' and bids his guests, and on that day will punish 'all such as are clothed with strange apparel' — a striking double parallel to the prepared feast (22:4) AND the man cast out for improper garment (22:11-13). Likely source for the wedding-clothing judgment.

echoes.text: Wisdom has built her house. She has carved out her seven pillars. She has prepared her meat. She has mixed her wine. She has also set her table. She has sent out her maidens. She cries from the highest places of the city: “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” As for him who is void of understanding, she says to him, “Come, eat some of my bread, Drink some of the wine which I have mixed! Leave your simple ways, and live. Walk in the way of […]
echoes.note: Wisdom builds her house, 'kills her beasts,' mixes her wine, and sends out maidservants to invite the simple to her feast — close structural echo of slaughtered cattle (22:4) and servants sent to call guests (22:3-4,9).

echoes.text: Yet he sent prophets to them, to bring them again to Yahweh; and they testified against them: but they would not give ear. The Spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you disobey the commandments of Yahweh, so that you can’t prosper? Because you have forsaken Yahweh, he has also forsaken you.’” They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the […]
echoes.note: Prophets/servants sent to call Israel back are seized and killed (Zechariah stoned in the temple court) — the king's servants beaten and murdered (22:6) figure the rejected prophets, a deuteronomistic pattern Matthew develops (cf. 23:34-37).

echoes.text: Since the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them: yet they didn’t listen to me, nor inclined their ear, but made their neck stiff: they did worse than their fathers.
echoes.note: God 'sent unto you all my servants the prophets... yet they hearkened not' but treated them shamefully — the repeated sending of servants who are spurned and killed (22:3-6) reuses this prophetic-rejection schema.

echoes.text: There be many created, but few shall be saved.
echoes.note: 'Many have been created, but few shall be saved' (Fourth Ezra) — a near-formulaic Second Temple parallel to 'many are called, but few are chosen' (22:14).

echoes.text: “Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat! Yes, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price. Why do you spend money for that which is not bread? and your labor for that which doesn’t satisfy? listen diligently to me, and eat you that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.
echoes.note: Open invitation to come freely to a banquet of rich food — thematic echo of the wide call to the highways (22:9), the unworthy invited replaced by all comers.

echoes.text: “Nevertheless they were disobedient, and rebelled against you, and cast your law behind their back, and killed your prophets that testified against them to turn them again to you, and they committed awful blasphemies.
echoes.note: Israel 'slew thy prophets which testified against them' — same servants-as-prophets motif behind the murdered messengers (22:6).

echoes.text: He burnt Yahweh’s house, and the king’s house; and all the houses of Jerusalem, even every great house, burnt he with fire.
echoes.note: Burning of the rebellious city (Jerusalem by Babylon) — the king sends armies, destroys the murderers and burns their city (22:7), echoing the prophetic-historical pattern of a city torched in judgment.

echoes.text: I will greatly rejoice in Yahweh, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decks himself with a garland, and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.
echoes.note: 'He hath clothed me with the garments of salvation... as a bridegroom decketh himself' — wedding-garment imagery (22:11-12) as the required clothing of righteousness/salvation for the marriage feast.

notes.text: O Lord — The prophet reflecting upon those great and glorious prophecies which he had delivered, interrupts the course of his prophecies, and breaks forth into a solemn celebration of God's wonderful works. Thy counsels - From which all thy works proceed, and which thou hast from time to time revealed to thy prophets and people, which were of old, being conceived from all eternity, are true and firm, and shall certainly be accomplished.

A city — Which is put for cities: or of enemies of God and his people. And under the name cities he comprehends their countries and kingdoms. Strangers - The royal cities, in which were the palaces of strangers, of Gentiles. No city - Their cities and palaces have been or shall be utterly and irrecoverably destroyed.
Shall fear — Thy stoutest enemies observing thy wonderful works, shall be converted, or at least forced to tremble before thee.
For — For thou hast defended thy poor and helpless people. As a storm - Makes a great noise, but without any effect.

The noise — The tumultuous noise, as the word properly signifies; the rage and furious attempts of those Heathen nations that fought against God's people. As the heat - With as much ease as thou dost allay the heat of a dry place, by the shadow of thy clouds, or by the rain which falls from black and shadowy clouds. The branch - The arm or power, as a branch is the arm of a tree.

And — In Mount Zion, in God's church. All people - Both Jews and Gentiles. A feast - A feast made up of the most delicate provisions, which is manifestly meant of the ordinances, graces, and comforts given by God in his church. Of wines - Which have continued upon the lees a competent time, whereby they gain strength, and are afterwards drawn off, and refined.
The face — The covering of the face. The veil - The ignorance of God, and of the true religion, which then was upon the Gentiles, and now is upon the Jews.

He — Christ will by his death destroy the power of death, take away the sting of the first death, and prevent the second. In victory - Hebrew. unto victory; so as to overcome it perfectly; which complete victory Christ hath already purchased for, and will in due time actually confer upon his people. Rebuke - The reproach and contempt cast upon his faithful people by the ungodly world.
Our God — Our Messiah, long since promised, and for whom we have waited long, is come into the world, bringing salvation with him.

glossa.text: *Amen.* ((HIER.)) A Hebrew word, which the Lord often uses in the Gospel: *Amen, amen,* that is, truly, truly, *I say to you.*

*A city.* Overthrown by Nabuchodonosor, it was restored by Nehemias and by Jesus the high priest. Overthrown by the Romans, it was restored by Aelius Hadrian; but not in the same place, nor to its former state.

*And for ever.* ((ID.)) That the fable of the thousand years' reign and of the golden and jewelled Jerusalem may rest.

notes.text: Lie down — To repose myself at noon, as the manner was in those hot countries. Green - Where there is both delight and plenty of provisions.
Restoreth — Hebrew. He bringeth it back; from its errors and wandering. For - Not for any worth in me, but for the glory of his justice, and faithfulness, and goodness.
Thy rod and thy staff — Two words denoting the same thing, and both designing God's pastoral care over him.

A table — Thou furnishest me with plenty of provisions and comforts. Oil - With aromatic ointments, which were then used at great feasts; thy comforts delight my soul. Runneth over - Thou hast given me a plentiful portions, signified by the cup, given to the guests by the master of the feast. This psalm is generally thought to have been composed by David, upon bringing the ark of God from the house of Obed- edom, into the tabernacle which David had built for it, 2 Sam. vi, 12, 17. Wherein he hath a farther prospect to the temple, which he earnestly desired and intended to build. Moreover because the tabernacle, and temple, and ark, were types of Christ, and of his church and of heaven. David extended his thoughts to them also, or at least the Holy Ghost designed to comprehend them under these typical expressions. He shews God's sovereignty over the world, ver. 1, 2. Who shall receive his blessing, ver. 3-6. An exhortation to receive Christ, ver. 7-10. A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *A psalm of David.* ((CASS.)) The Prophet foretold the return of the people from Babylon. *The Lord ruleth me.* A psalm of mercy, enumerating ten graces, that all may hope in the mercy of God. ((AUG.)) The Church speaks of Christ.

*In a place of pasture.* ((CASS.)) The first grace, a place of pasture, that is, the divine word, which fattens those who meditate upon it. *Upon the water.* The second grace, the water of refreshment.

*My soul.* ((ID.)) The third grace, etc., *as far as* but first he brought me up upon the water of refreshment, first he converted my soul. *He hath led.* ((ID.)) The fourth, in that he led me upon the precepts of charity. *Upon the paths.* ((AUG.)) The narrower commandments and the more perfect counsels; as it were upon paths few just men walk, even as paths are narrower than roads.

*For though I shall walk.* ((CASS.)) The fifth, that in the shadow of death he fears no evils. *Thou art with me.* ((AUG.)) In the heart by faith, that after the shadow of death I may be with thee. *Thy rod.* ((CASS.)) The sixth, correction; or the rod is strictness, which converts vices. The staff is governance, which upholds the faithful.

*Thou hast prepared in my sight.* ((CASS.)) The seventh, the table of the Lord, the blessed banqueting, the fullness of faith, the heavenly food, of which the Apostle: *He that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh judgment to himself. In my sight a table:* even if not that of the wicked. Of this it is said: *But these at the table of the rich man,* that is, of Christ, *know that thou too must prepare the like,* that is, to suffer as he did. *Thou hast anointed:* the eighth, the anointing of the head, namely of Christ, which was dried up by no barrenness of sin, whence the rest of the members rejoice, because from the head the ointment ran down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, and unto the skirt of his garment. *And my chalice.* The ninth, the chalice, the blood of Christ, which so inebriates that it makes men sober. *Mine,* because I receive it. Or, thine, because thou givest it. The table and the chalice, flesh and blood, although they are one sacrament, yet under diverse species, because both are taken, are here set down separately.
*And mercy.* ((CASS.)) The tenth, mercy following after unto keeping, which goes before unto the conferring of grace.
*And that I may dwell.* ((HIER.)) This is joined to all the things above. As though: thou hast placed, thou hast brought up, thou hast led, etc., and this to the end that I may dwell.

notes.text: So stand — As ye have done hitherto.
I beseech — He repeats this twice, as if speaking to each face to face, and that with the utmost tenderness.

And I entreat thee also, true yokefellow — St. Paul had many fellowlabourers, but not many yokefellows. In this number was Barnabas first, and then Silas, whom he probably addresses here; for Silas had been his yokefellow at the very place, Acts xvi, 19. Help those women who laboured together with me - Literally, who wrestled. The Greek word doth not imply preaching, or anything of that kind; but danger and toil endured for the sake of the gospel, which was also endured at the same time, probably at Philippi, by Clement and my other fellowlabourers - This is a different word from the former, and does properly imply fellowpreachers. Whose names, although not set down here, are in the book of life - As are those of all believers. An allusion to the wrestlers in the Olympic games, whose names were all enrolled in a book. Reader, is thy name there? Then walk circumspectly, lest the Lord blot thee out of his book!

Let your gentleness — Yieldingness, sweetness of temper, the result of joy in the Lord. Be known - By your whole behaviour. To all men - Good and bad, gentle and froward. Those of the roughest tempers are good natured to some, from natural sympathy and various motives; a Christian, to all. The Lord - The judge, the rewarder, the avenger. Is at hand - Standeth at the door.

Be anxiously careful for nothing — If men are not gentle towards you, yet neither on this, nor any other account, be careful, but pray. Carefulness and prayer cannot stand together. In every thing - Great and small. Let your requests be made known - They who by a preposterous shame or distrustful modesty, cover, stifle, or keep in their desires, as if they were either too small or too great, must be racked with care; from which they are entirely delivered, who pour them out with a free and filial confidence. To God - It is not always proper to disclose them to men. By supplication - Which is the enlarging upon and pressing our petition. With thanksgiving - The surest mark of a soul free from care, and of prayer joined with true resignation. This is always followed by peace. Peace and thanksgiving are both coupled together, Colossians iii, 15.

And the peace of God — That calm, heavenly repose, that tranquility of spirit, which God only can give. Which surpasseth all understanding - Which none can comprehend, save he that receiveth it. Shall keep - Shall guard, as a garrison does a city. Your hearts - Your affections. Your minds - Your understandings, and all the various workings of them; through the Spirit and power of Christ Jesus, in the knowledge and love of God. Without a guard set on these likewise, the purity and vigour of our affections cannot long be preserved.

Finally — To sum up all. Whatsoever things are true - Here are eight particulars placed in two fourfold rows; the former containing their duty; the latter, the commendation of it. The first word in the former row answers the first in the latter; the second word, the second and so on. True - In speech. Honest - In action. Just - With regard to others. Pure - With regard to yourselves. Lovely - And what more lovely than truth? Of good report - As is honesty, even where it is not practiced. If there be any virtue - And all virtues are contained in justice. If there be any praise - In those things which relate rather to ourselves than to our neighbour. Think on these things - That ye may both practice them yourselves, and recommend them to others.

The things which ye have learned — As catechumens. And received - By continual instructions. And heard and seen - In my life and conversation. These do, and the God of peace shall be with you - Not only the peace of God, but God himself, the fountain of peace.

glossa.text: *Joy, and consolation.* That is, through whom I am gladdened in the present and shall be crowned in the future. For when the disciples are victors in the contest, the master will be worthy of the crown.
*I beseech Evodia,* etc. I admonish all, but especially Evodia and Syntyche: because these religious women were wont to receive preachers.

*Names.* They who are distinguished by merits shall have diverse mansions in the eternal house. Whence: *In my Father's house there are many mansions ((Joan. XIV))*. *The book of life.* The predestination in which all who are to be saved have been predestined. As if: Do not, O Philippians, take it hard that I have not named you all one by one in my epistle, for although you are not written in it, yet in the book of life you are contained.

*Rejoice,* etc. Being gladdened over their faith and their works, the Apostle, that they may be the more eager, desires that they, advancing in this zeal, should rejoice in the Lord, and he repeats it, that he may show that he truly rejoices in them.

*Moderation.* That is, right measure, so that all joy may be in the Lord, and that others may learn this through you. Or, *let moderation be known to all,* faithful and unbelieving, that they may imitate it, lest they be able to reprehend. *The Lord is nigh,* that is, ready to give whatsoever is needful in spiritual or in temporal things. Be solicitous and fearful about nothing. But your petitions concerning those things which you wish to obtain.

*But in every prayer.* Prayer and supplication are made in common for oneself or for others, concerning whatsoever things, but petition is made concerning things necessary by name. *Let them be made known.* This making known comes about by assiduity, and by watchfulness of prayer. Then at last peace keeps the hearts in Christ. He says this for this reason, because he who has peace with God does not fear an adverse mind. *With God.* Or to the angels, who offer them to God. Whence: When you were praying, I offered your prayer before God. Or, let them be made known for us with God through endurance, not with men through boasting.

*And the peace of God,* that is, God, who is the highest peace, which cannot even be thought, and therefore outside him there is need of nothing. *It surpasseth all understanding.* Ours, not that of those who always behold the face of the Father. Or, the peace whereby God himself is at peace *surmounts all understanding:* except his own, because neither can we know it thus, nor can any angels.

*For the rest, brethren,* etc. Thus far he has admonished against persecutors and against false preachers. But for the rest, in the conclusion, he sets forth the things which belong to perfection. *Whatsoever things are just.* This toward one's neighbour. *Holy,* in one's own life; and, that a lesser thing be named, *whatsoever things are lovely,* that is, worthy to be loved, as a modest gait, humble speech and the like.

*Of good report. ((AUG.))* For ourselves our own life, for others a good report is necessary. Accordingly whosoever guards his life from the crimes of shameful deeds does well to himself; but whosoever [guards] his good report is merciful toward others also.

notes.text: Jesus answering, spake — That is, spake with reference to what had just past.
A king, who made a marriage feast for his son — So did God, when he brought his first - begotten into the world.
Them that were invited — Namely, the Jews.
Fatlings — Fatted beasts and fowls.
One to his farm, another to his merchandise — One must mind what he has; another, gain what he wants. How many perish by misusing lawful things!
The king sending forth his troops — The Roman armies employed of God for that purpose. Destroyed those murderers - Primarily the Jews.
Go into the highways — The word properly signifies, the by- ways, or turnings of the road.
They gathered all — By preaching everwhere.
The guest — The members of the visible Church.
A wedding garment — The righteousness of Christ, first imputed, then implanted. It may easily be observed, this has no relation to the Lord's Supper, but to God's proceeding at the last day.
Many are called; few chosen — Many hear; few believe. Yea, many are members of the visible, but few of the invisible Church. Matt. xx, 16.

glossa.text: *It was made like.* Again he convicts them by parables: he is not silent because they are exasperated, but by another parable he tells them that a worse anger of God is to come. *A marriage feast.* The bridal chamber of the marriage is the virgin's womb. Of those invited to the marriage Matthew alone tells. Luke tells another likeness in part, of a supper, that is, of the eternal banquet, from which no one who has entered is driven out, as he is from the present Church.

*The oxen.* Because first the prophets, and afterwards the apostles, suffered from unbelievers: who are now to you for an example of what you must believe. Come, by faith, by agreeing with the rest. The oxen are the fathers of the Old Testament, to whom leave was granted to strike their enemies as with a horn. The fatlings, from feeding, that is, the heralds of the New Testament, fat with inward charity, seeking things on high on the wing of contemplation. Slain, either from what they had been, or already set in rest through the death of the flesh.
*Another to his farm.* To go to a farm is to lie immoderately upon earthly labour. But to trade is to gape after earthly gains.

*And the king.* Above, he was a man while he was inviting and doing works of clemency, now in taking vengeance he is king only . *And having sent,* etc. Having sent his armies, that is, the angels by whom he will exercise judgment, he destroys the persecutors: and the city, that is, the flesh in which they dwelt, he will burn with the soul in hell.

*The marriage indeed is ready.* The whole sacrament of the incarnation is accomplished, the nativity and the passion.

*To the outgoings,* etc. Actions are the ways: the outgoings are the failing of actions: because for the most part those are easily converted whom no prosperity attends in earthly doings.

*That he might see the guests.* That is, that he may make the merits of those to be judged be seen, and may discern them. *Not clothed with a wedding garment.* Now, the Pharisees having been refuted, he adds that not all who are in the Church are worthy of the kingdom, lest his own grow slothful.
*Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment?* A friend, because invited to the marriage. *How,* he convicts him of shamelessness.

*His hands and feet being bound.* They are bound by punishment who here would not be bound from evil, that is, restrained. The hands which were not stretched out to almsgiving. The feet slow to good. There each several member shall be subjected to punishments, which here served each several vice. *Outer,* etc. Because here they have the inward darkness of the heart.

*But many are called, but few chosen.* One being cast out, in whom the whole body of the wicked is set forth, a general sentence is brought in. *But many are called.* As though he should say: Even if I have spoken of one, it is to be understood of many.

echoes.text: The crowns shall be to Helem, and to Tobijah, and to Jedaiah, and to Hen the son of Zephaniah, for a memorial in Yahweh’s temple.
echoes.note: Paul's calling the Philippians his 'crown' (stephanos) echoes the prophetic image of a crown laid up as a memorial and reward in the temple, and more broadly the OT crown-of-glory motif (Isaiah 28:5; 62:3). Volume is faint and the metaphor is conventional, but coherence with the eschatological reward imagery available in the prophets supports a low-grade echo.

echoes.text: You shall also be a crown of beauty in the hand of Yahweh, and a royal diadem in the hand of your God.
echoes.note: 'You shall be a crown of beauty in the hand of the LORD' supplies the figural background for Paul's 'my joy and crown,' where a redeemed community is the eschatological adornment of its caretaker. Recurrence of the crown-of-glory image across Isaiah (28:5; 62:3) makes it available, though the volume here is low and the trope generic.

echoes.text: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers;
echoes.note: The exhortation to 'stand firm in the Lord' draws on the OT contrast between the stable righteous, planted and unmoved, and the chaff-like wicked. Coherence with the steadfastness motif (Psalm 1:3; 112:6) is real, but the volume is faint and 'stand firm' is too diffuse to anchor a single source, so this is a contested echo.

echoes.text: Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin—and if not, please blot me out of your book which you have written.”
echoes.note: Paul's claim that his fellow workers' 'names are in the book of life' alludes directly to Moses' plea to be blotted out of 'the book you have written,' the founding OT text of the heavenly register. Volume is high (the explicit book-of-life image), availability is secure in the Torah, and coherence with Paul's confidence in the Philippians' salvation is strong.

echoes.text: Let them be blotted out of the book of life, and not be written with the righteous.
echoes.note: 'Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not enrolled among the righteous' provides the precise phrase 'book of life/living' that Paul reverses into a positive assurance. High volume on the shared lexeme, strong recurrence of the register motif across the Psalter and prophets, and thematic coherence with the contrast of the saved versus the lost.

echoes.text: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book.
echoes.note: Daniel's eschatological promise that 'everyone whose name is found written in the book' shall be delivered supplies the apocalyptic deliverance sense Paul gives the image. Availability in Second-Temple apocalyptic and coherence with the resurrection hope of Philippians 3 make this a strong contributor to Paul's 'book of life.'

echoes.text: Then those who feared Yahweh spoke one with another; and Yahweh listened, and heard, and a book of memory was written before him, for those who feared Yahweh, and who honored his name.
echoes.note: 'A book of remembrance was written before him of those who feared the LORD' offers the motif of a heavenly ledger recording the faithful by name, coherent with Paul's naming of co-laborers whose names stand recorded. Volume is moderate (remembrance-book rather than 'book of life'), but recurrence within the register tradition supports the link.

echoes.text: You number my wanderings. You put my tears into your bottle. Aren’t they in your book?
echoes.note: 'Are they not in your book?' adds another instance of the divine record motif, reinforcing the availability and recurrence of the heavenly-book tradition Paul invokes. Low volume and no shared 'life' lexeme make it a faint contributing echo rather than a primary source.

echoes.text: Yahweh is near to all those who call on him, to all who call on him in truth.
echoes.note: 'The Lord is at hand' (ho kyrios engys) most closely matches 'The LORD is near to all who call on him' (engys kyrios), grounding Paul's nearness claim and its link to prayer in v.6. High lexical volume on engys, coherence with the prayer/petition context, and availability in the LXX Psalter make this the strongest source for the phrase.

echoes.text: Be glad in Yahweh, and rejoice, you righteous! Shout for joy, all you who are upright in heart!
echoes.note: 'Rejoice in the LORD always' echoes the recurrent Psalter imperative 'Be glad in the LORD, and rejoice, you righteous' (32:11; cf. 33:1; 97:12). Recurrence is strong across the Psalter and coherence with Paul's joy theme is high; volume is moderate because Paul universalizes 'always' beyond any single psalm.

echoes.text: Be glad in Yahweh, you righteous people! Give thanks to his holy Name.
echoes.note: 'Rejoice in the LORD, O you righteous' supplies the same divine-object joy imperative that Paul doubles for emphasis. The Psalter's habitual call to rejoice in the LORD is available and coherent, though the volume of any single verse is moderate given the formula's diffusion.

echoes.text: Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.
echoes.note: 'The LORD is near to the brokenhearted' reinforces the 'Lord is near' motif with the same engys idiom, and Psalm 34 broadly underwrites Paul's confidence in deliverance. Recurrence of the nearness formula with Psalm 145 strengthens coherence, though volume per verse is moderate.

echoes.text: Be silent at the presence of the Lord Yahweh, for the day of Yahweh is at hand. For Yahweh has prepared a sacrifice. He has consecrated his guests.
echoes.note: 'The day of the LORD is at hand/near' supplies the eschatological-imminence sense of 'The Lord is at hand,' if Paul means the Lord's coming rather than his presence. Availability in the prophetic day-of-the-Lord tradition and coherence with Philippians' Parousia hope (3:20) support this, though it competes with the Psalter nearness reading.

echoes.text: You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.
echoes.note: 'You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you' parallels Paul's 'peace of God which surpasses all understanding will guard your hearts,' linking divine peace, the mind, and protective keeping. Coherence is strong on the guarding-peace-of-the-mind motif; volume is moderate because Paul does not quote the phrasing verbatim.

echoes.text: Cast your burden on Yahweh, and he will sustain you. He will never allow the righteous to be moved.
echoes.note: 'Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you' parallels Paul's remedy for anxiety: hand your requests to God in prayer rather than carry them. Coherence with the anti-anxiety-through-petition logic is strong; volume is moderate since Paul shares the idea, not the wording.

echoes.text: In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you, Yahweh alone, make me live in safety.
echoes.note: 'In peace I will both lie down and sleep, for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety' offers the OT pairing of divine peace with security from anxiety that underlies 'do not be anxious... and the peace of God will guard you.' Volume is low and the link thematic, so this is a contributing echo.

echoes.text: Anxiety in a man’s heart weighs it down, but a kind word makes it glad.
echoes.note: 'Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad' supplies a wisdom backdrop for Paul's 'in nothing be anxious.' Volume and verbal overlap are slight, but the heart-anxiety theme is available in the sapiential tradition, making this a faint echo.

echoes.text: And if a man loves righteousness, The fruits of wisdom’s labor are virtues, For she teaches soberness and understanding, righteousness and courage; And there is nothing in life for men more profitable than these.
echoes.note: Wisdom's praise of the cardinal virtues ('she teaches self-control and prudence, justice and courage') models the Hellenistic-Jewish virtue list Paul adapts, especially the terms for 'just' and the framing of virtue (arete) itself, which Paul uses uniquely here. Coherence with the Wisdom tradition's moral catalogues makes this a plausible deuterocanonical source.

echoes.text: He who loves purity of heart and speaks gracefully is the king’s friend.
echoes.note: Paul's virtue catalogue (true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, of good report) draws on the sapiential ideal of the pure heart and gracious speech that wins favor. Recurrence of these virtue terms in Proverbs and the wider Hellenistic-Jewish moral tradition supplies availability, but the volume of any one verse is low.

echoes.text: So you will find favor, and good understanding in the sight of God and man.
echoes.note: 'So you will find favor and good repute (LXX: good things) in the sight of God and man' parallels Paul's 'whatever is of good report' and the appeal to public commendation. Volume is low and the link conceptual, but the good-repute motif is available in the sapiential tradition.

echoes.text: You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.
echoes.note: 'The God of peace will be with you' continues the divine-peace motif of v.7 and resonates with Isaiah's promise that God keeps in peace those whose minds are fixed on him. Volume is faint here and the title 'God of peace' is Paul's own, so this is a low-grade continuation echo of the peace tradition.

echoes.text: Then Gideon built an altar there to Yahweh, and called it “Yahweh is Peace.” To this day it is still in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
echoes.note: Gideon's altar 'The LORD is peace' (YHWH-shalom) offers an OT antecedent for naming God by his peace, loosely behind Paul's 'the God of peace.' The volume is very low and the connection figural, but it documents the availability of associating God's name with shalom.

echoes.text: In this mountain, Yahweh of Armies will make all peoples a feast of fat things, a feast of choice wines, of fat things full of marrow, of well refined choice wines.
echoes.note: The eschatological banquet — the LORD makes 'a feast of fat things' (fatlings/oxen killed, 22:4) for all peoples on his mountain. The king's marriage feast for his son draws on this prophetic image of the messianic/end-time banquet; the killing of fatlings matches Isaiah's 'fat things full of marrow.'

echoes.text: Be silent at the presence of the Lord Yahweh, for the day of Yahweh is at hand. For Yahweh has prepared a sacrifice. He has consecrated his guests. It will happen in the day of Yahweh’s sacrifice, that I will punish the princes, the king’s sons, and all those who are clothed with foreign clothing.
echoes.note: The LORD 'has prepared a sacrifice' and bids his guests, and on that day will punish 'all such as are clothed with strange apparel' — a striking double parallel to the prepared feast (22:4) AND the man cast out for improper garment (22:11-13). Likely source for the wedding-clothing judgment.

echoes.text: Wisdom has built her house. She has carved out her seven pillars. She has prepared her meat. She has mixed her wine. She has also set her table. She has sent out her maidens. She cries from the highest places of the city: “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” As for him who is void of understanding, she says to him, “Come, eat some of my bread, Drink some of the wine which I have mixed! Leave your simple ways, and live. Walk in the way of […]
echoes.note: Wisdom builds her house, 'kills her beasts,' mixes her wine, and sends out maidservants to invite the simple to her feast — close structural echo of slaughtered cattle (22:4) and servants sent to call guests (22:3-4,9).

echoes.text: Yet he sent prophets to them, to bring them again to Yahweh; and they testified against them: but they would not give ear. The Spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you disobey the commandments of Yahweh, so that you can’t prosper? Because you have forsaken Yahweh, he has also forsaken you.’” They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the […]
echoes.note: Prophets/servants sent to call Israel back are seized and killed (Zechariah stoned in the temple court) — the king's servants beaten and murdered (22:6) figure the rejected prophets, a deuteronomistic pattern Matthew develops (cf. 23:34-37).

echoes.text: Since the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them: yet they didn’t listen to me, nor inclined their ear, but made their neck stiff: they did worse than their fathers.
echoes.note: God 'sent unto you all my servants the prophets... yet they hearkened not' but treated them shamefully — the repeated sending of servants who are spurned and killed (22:3-6) reuses this prophetic-rejection schema.

echoes.text: There be many created, but few shall be saved.
echoes.note: 'Many have been created, but few shall be saved' (Fourth Ezra) — a near-formulaic Second Temple parallel to 'many are called, but few are chosen' (22:14).

echoes.text: “Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat! Yes, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price. Why do you spend money for that which is not bread? and your labor for that which doesn’t satisfy? listen diligently to me, and eat you that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.
echoes.note: Open invitation to come freely to a banquet of rich food — thematic echo of the wide call to the highways (22:9), the unworthy invited replaced by all comers.

echoes.text: “Nevertheless they were disobedient, and rebelled against you, and cast your law behind their back, and killed your prophets that testified against them to turn them again to you, and they committed awful blasphemies.
echoes.note: Israel 'slew thy prophets which testified against them' — same servants-as-prophets motif behind the murdered messengers (22:6).

echoes.text: He burnt Yahweh’s house, and the king’s house; and all the houses of Jerusalem, even every great house, burnt he with fire.
echoes.note: Burning of the rebellious city (Jerusalem by Babylon) — the king sends armies, destroys the murderers and burns their city (22:7), echoing the prophetic-historical pattern of a city torched in judgment.

echoes.text: I will greatly rejoice in Yahweh, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decks himself with a garland, and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.
echoes.note: 'He hath clothed me with the garments of salvation... as a bridegroom decketh himself' — wedding-garment imagery (22:11-12) as the required clothing of righteousness/salvation for the marriage feast.
